title: How to Use AI Memory Effectively for Domain-Specific Tasks
summary: Effective Agent memory requires deliberate choices about what the system should learn and how that learning informs downstream action. We built our own deal-memory system at Hindsight (but you might not have to).
body_markdown:
Adding learning capabilities to your Agents has never been easier thanks to general-purpose memory libraries, like Mem0, Zep, Vectorize, and past.dev, which can supply much of the infrastructure.


It may be tempting to add one of these libraries to your agents - but if you’re building domain-specific agents for your customers or team-wide memory, we find that out-of-the-box implementations might not go far enough.


We found that accurate event interpretation, observation synthesis, and downstream retrieval require careful consideration and engineering work.


We’ve been building deal-specific memory at Hindsight. This blog explores the decisions behind our system and what a builder should configure in a library vs. build themselves today. GTM is the illustration; the broader question is how to make memory useful for your agents and your product’s domain.


> **TL;DR.** We suggest working backwards from the decisions your agents will be making. Build an interpretation pipeline for your domain, start synthesis with the dimensions that matter most, and retrieve against those same conditions.


> For advanced teams, add learning loops that evaluate whether applying Memory improves outcomes.


## Retrieval is not the same as judgment


In early 2023, we were building general retrieval infrastructure (RAG) at my first startup, Baseplate. For us, retrieving external context was the starting point for giving agents something resembling memory.


A RAG-powered agent could answer a question like “How should I position against this competitor?” by identifying deals against that competitor and using RAG to find specific positioning examples that live in a database. We built it, and reps actually loved it.


But sales leaders saw missing judgement. One leader described the difference as A players versus B players.


- A B player follows the playbook and repeats what others have done.
- An A player studies comparable situations, judges what worked or could improve, and forms a perspective for this buyer.


Retrieving a statement doesn’t actually answer the question of how a rep should position in a specific scenario. It repeats what someone else did.


This has the counterproductive effect of reinforcing the status quo, for better or worse. We saw this repeatedly with initial versions of Hindsight. Teams would build battlecards using evidence from deals, basically summarizing what their teams were already doing instead of learning from it.


This was one limitation we ran into when trying to turn retrieval into useful business advice. Luckily, we’re not in 2023 anymore—models, tool calling, reasoning, and retrieval look meaningfully different.


Memory systems don’t just capture events like a RAG system would; they also need to interpret them. That interpretation process differs greatly between a support chat thread and a B2B deal with multiple touchpoints, conversations, and characters.


## The four concepts of agent memory


Memory platforms provide increasingly capable extraction, consolidation, and retrieval. Vectorize, Zep, Mem0, and Past.dev illustrate overlapping approaches. I find four general concepts useful for developers looking to understand that infrastructure.


1. **Event Capture.** Every memory system starts with Events. That could be a chat thread, a call transcript, or the touchpoints across a deal. Designing the event is the foundation. What context do you need? And how do you maintain provenance? Do you need source context at retrieval time or will synthesized memory suffice? See how[Past.dev makes timestamped sources](https://www.past.dev/docs/memory-api/concepts) and supporting excerpts central to its model.
2. **Event Interpretation.** Run event context through an LLM to produce useful statements or assessments, which we call Observations. We highly recommend designing this pipeline for your domain: a support exchange and a months-long deal may need radically different interpretation.[Mem0 lets you customize extraction](https://docs.mem0.ai/open-source/features/custom-instructions) or[store externally interpreted content](https://docs.mem0.ai/core-concepts/how-it-works) ;[Vectorize also exposes extraction controls](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/configuration) . For domain-specific agents, we recommend owning the design and evaluation of this interpretation layer. You might configure a library, build specialized agents around it, or combine both approaches.
3. **Synthesis.** Across Observations, we look for patterns and emerging trends, which we’ll call Learnings. Think deeply about what should be grouped together by identifying the key dimensions. Do we need to aggregate learnings by subscription status, account type, deal segment, use case, or something else? Start with the most important dimensions and expand as you can evaluate the results.[Vectorize supports custom consolidation instructions](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/observations) for different scopes;[Mem0’s hosted Dream](https://docs.mem0.ai/platform/features/dream) also synthesizes patterns.
4. **Retrieval.** Agents need access to Learnings, Observations, and/or Events at runtime. Define what makes an experience relevant to the decision before choosing the search technique. Metadata filters, semantic matching, reranking, and application logic can work together. Access permissions and analytical relevance are separate requirements.


A library can provide much of this infrastructure for new projects. If we were starting Hindsight fresh today, we would evaluate which pre-built layers to adopt. But we would still make the same domain decisions about event boundaries, interpretation, synthesis, and retrieval. Those decisions can live in configuration, in agents around the library, or across both.

The memory primitives stay the same. The decision determines what each stage needs to preserve.


## Example: a support request


Let’s compare 2 types of events: a support thread vs. a B2B software deal.


Let’s say Amy asks for a refund. Here’s how that experience could become useful memory:


1. **Event.** Account verification fails because Amy doesn’t have a membership account. We verify her purchase using an order confirmation instead and issue store credit at her request.
2. **Observations.** Retain the specific facts: Amy prefers store credit, account verification failed, and order confirmation provided a successful alternative.
3. **Learning.** Across similar cases, we might identify a pattern: customers without membership accounts need a different verification path. That’s a broader hypothesis, separate from Amy’s personal preference.
4. **Application and evaluation.** Offer that path earlier in comparable cases, then measure whether it improves resolution. The result becomes evidence for the next round of Learnings.


The event has a clear sequence and resolution. We can see which intervention worked and what would need testing before turning it into a general procedure.


Amy’s refund request


One interaction. Two different kinds of memory.


01

Amy has no membership account.


02

An alternative verification path works.


03

Amy requests this resolution.


Personal observation


Amy prefers store credit.


Retain for future interactions with Amy.


Broader hypothesis


Customers without membership accounts may need a different verification path.


Look for evidence across similar cases.


Test offering order-confirmation verification earlier. Measure whether it improves resolution, then update the Learning.


Illustrative example: an individual preference is an observation; a reusable procedure needs evidence and evaluation.


## Example: a B2B deal


Other events might not be so simple. Let’s say we’re working on a B2B deal with Acme Corp. that spans months of calls, emails, CRM notes, and different stakeholders.


- The event itself is complex and originates across multiple sources. We may need to prioritize specific emails and call transcripts. The call transcripts themselves need interpretation: Acme’s buyers often hide what they’re thinking.
- Interpretation is even more complex. An LLM would have to interpret these unclear events to produce an Observation like “Sam, the IT buyer, had his security objection effectively handled during the demo by doing X.” We need more reasoning and context (like objection handling guides and security documentation) to know what “effective” here means.
- Synthesis requires building a model of how these observations should connect to other deals. We need to aggregate by competitive scenario, buyer personas, deal segments, and more.


Acme Corp. · One deal, many sources


The event is the full buying journey, reconstructed over months.

Was Sam’s security objection handled effectively?


Assess the buyer’s response against evidence and a rubric. A mention of security alone doesn’t answer the question.

Buyer persona

Which dimensions matter most depends on the decision in the current deal.


Illustrative example: deal interpretation needs source context and domain judgment before an observation can inform another deal.


## How we built Deal Memory


These factors fundamentally change how we build each part of the system, and where we spend our tokens and engineering effort. I’ll illustrate below how we approached it so you can see what makes sense for your product.


1. **Event Capture.** We treat the full deal as the event, rather than an individual document, and update it as the deal progresses. The deal is reconstructed as a timeline, with each touchpoint available in full. Some Deals don’t fit in context windows (millions of tokens) so we may pre-summarize and embed documents. Some context doesn’t exist in the records, so we fill gaps by asking for additional inputs.
2. **Interpretation.** A single summarization prompt wasn’t enough for our task - we needed to fully own and implement the interpretation layer with an Agent system. Useful Observations in our use case required the deal context alongside sales playbooks, rubrics, and product taxonomy. We built a Deal Review Agent with an orchestrator and specialized subagents for analysis dimensions like execution, product, pricing, and competition, then reconciled their findings into a deal story and observations. You could build that analysis around a memory library; our design reflects the judgments we needed, rather than a limitation of every library.
3. **Synthesis.** We need cohort-specific analysis by dimensions like persona, account type, segment, product, and competitor - adapting to unique CRM schemas and customer-specific needs. This is run by a Data Analysis agent that has access to a sandbox to run exploratory data analysis (EDA) and aggregations across key dimensions. For teams getting started, pick the 2-3 dimensions most likely to change the action, then expand as evidence supports it. This builds towards a working world model with revisable expectations about what might work in a new deal. User ID may be one of the least useful dimensions for learning across an organization.
4. **Retrieval.** Simple retrieval of memories failed for us because deals may match multiple cohorts of learnings that needed to be weighted differently based on the current scenario. For example, the current deal might be driven more by competition and less influenced by factors like account type. So we built our own retrieval with ‘Comparable Deal Matching’ which combines semantic similarity with factors such as use case, persona, account type, segment, and competitor. Teams can tune those factors; matching a competitor alone may miss the buyer’s actual problem.


These choices give our agents the context and analysis to recommend or execute the “Next Best Step” for a specific deal. A builder could implement them with custom infrastructure, a configurable memory library, or a combination. What matters is whether the resulting memory supports the decision.


## Close the loop with evaluation


That still leaves effectiveness as a gray area. You might need to build your own evaluation system and loop to reach your self-driving vision. PostHog and Amplitude are building toward loops that connect product changes to measurement and experiments. We’re building our own evaluation system on top of Deal Memory and action-oriented workflows.


1. **Versioned playbooks.** This might be a set of skills, a set of markdown files in a git repo, or something like Playbooks in Hindsight. We need a system to take Learnings and turn them into hypotheses about how we should work to achieve our goals—in our case, win deals. Agents can compose and edit these versioned playbooks, with people approving changes to organizational procedures.
2. **Experimentation.** We need to apply our playbooks the way a PLG product team experiments with onboarding and CTAs. Identify a holdout group and a treatment group, and apply the published and experimental versions of your playbook to comparable cases. Some agent runs get the new one.
3. **Measurement and evals.** Identify the behavior we’re trying to change or the metric we’re trying to move. This could be qualitative, like better customer discovery, but we need a way to assess it. We use LLM judges to score custom metrics from 1–5 and collect user feedback as well. Define acceptance criteria before the experiment, then evaluate once there’s enough evidence. If the new playbook meets those criteria, publish it as the canonical version.


These might seem like two different systems—memory and action. But they are closely linked in well-functioning systems. The same playbook we use to guide actions is used to interpret events. Interpretation and synthesis need to account for which version was followed, what actions were taken, and what happened next. Retrieval needs to find the right memory at the right granularity for the action. Results then feed back into the next round of Learnings.


1


Current deal + comparable experience


Retrieve the Learnings that apply to this scenario.


2


Versioned playbook + next best step


Recommend an action using the current approach and evidence.


3


Action + measured outcome


Track what was used, what happened, and which version guided it.


Feed the evidence back into interpretation, Learnings, and the next playbook version.


Memory and action improve together when outcomes become evidence for the next decision.


## What to adopt and what to build


Good memory systems save you tokens, improve your product experience, and move you towards self-improving systems that can outperform humans. The ‘holy grail’ for many application builders, and one of the few ways I can think of to build an enduring moat.


If our Agents can be the best at delivering the “Next Best Step to Win a Deal”, and improve over time, we win!


As Memory tools get better, you might be able to add them to your Agents too—with some careful consideration. We started building Hindsight’s memory system before most of these tools existed, but the general approaches across platforms have coalesced and you may be able to pick and choose what parts you actually need to extend vs. adopt as-is.


With a memory system built for your specific use case, you ensure Agents learn effectively and apply relevant learnings when needed. We can then track whether the recommended action was taken and what happened afterward. That evidence feeds back into interpretation, synthesis, and the next set of Learnings and updates.


For Deal Memory, the data is early. Over three months, we evaluated 10,000 deals, including 3,000 in the treatment group. We observed an 8% higher win rate in treatment relative to baseline, alongside improvements in memory quality and recall relevance. We’re continuing to investigate which buying scenarios benefit most and which changes contribute to the improvement.


We’re getting closer to the holy grail: an agent that can identify the Next Best Step like an A player, learn from what happens when it’s used, and share those Learnings with everyone else.
